references.section: Who must register or notify; process
references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] A food business must not operate before it is registered with, or has notified, the enforcement agency under the Food Act 2008. Local government environmental health services register cafes, restaurants, retail outlets, home-based food businesses, manufacturers, school canteens, childcare and mobile food vans (registered where the vehicle is kept overnight; temporary and mobile businesses also notify each other local government they trade in). The Department of Health registers businesses in Kings Park, on Rottnest Island and outside any local government area, and some exporters. Fees are one-off and set by each agency. Section 113 makes it an offence not to tell the agency about changes such as a sale or closure.
references.interpretation: Most WA food businesses register with their local government before trading. Captured on 2026-10-12 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] From 8 December 2023 category one businesses (that process unpackaged, potentially hazardous, ready-to-eat food, such as cafes, restaurants and caterers) and category two businesses (that minimally handle such food, such as delis and service stations) must ensure food handlers are trained, appoint at least one food safety supervisor reasonably available to advise and supervise, and (category one) keep records showing key controls are managed for at least 3 months. Supervisor certification must be refreshed every 5 years.
references.interpretation: WA food service and retail businesses handling unpackaged potentially hazardous food need a food safety supervisor and trained handlers. Captured on 2026-10-12 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Food businesses that want an outdoor dining area on public land such as a footpath need an Outdoor Dining Permit under the City of Perth Outdoor Dining Local Law 2019. Applicants must be a registered food business, provide public liability insurance of $20 million, and arrange furniture storage. There is no charge (from 1 February 2019). Provisional approval is given for two months and an officer arranges an inspection within 10 days.
references.interpretation: Using a footpath for dining needs a local government permit; the City of Perth is an example and other local governments have their own rules. Captured on 2026-10-12 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] All advertisement signage on private land requires City approval unless exempt under Schedule 9 of the local planning scheme. Exempt examples include business signs on non-residential buildings up to 5 square metres per wall and signs not visible from public space. A sign needs approval if it advertises goods or services not relevant to the site, is more than 3 metres above ground, or impedes a road or footpath.
references.interpretation: Business signs are controlled by each local government's planning scheme; the City of Busselton is an example. references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Skin penetration operators must comply with the Health (Skin Penetration Procedures) Regulations 1998 and the Code of Practice for Skin Penetration Procedures. Procedures include tattooing, piercing, scarification, branding, dermal anchors, waxing, electrolysis and acupuncture. Establishments must notify the local government of trading name, address and procedures, and give a layout of the premises before opening. Mobile practitioners may only work where each place is registered. Hand basins (hands-free for new fit-outs) and two sinks are required. Fines up to $1,000 plus daily penalties. Under the Children and Community Services Act 2004, tattooing a minor without written parental consent can bring a $12,000 fine and 1 year in prison; intimate piercing of a child $18,000 and 18 months.

rule_sets.title: Western Australia: business licences, insurance and tax
rule_sets.description: Registrations, licences, insurance and tax most WA businesses check: food registration, food safety supervisors, liquor, alfresco dining, signs, workers compensation and payroll tax.
limitations: Built from WA Department of Health, Racing, Gaming and Liquor, WorkCover WA, RevenueWA and local government web pages, not from the Acts themselves.
Does not decide which liquor licence you need, or whether you can trade under an exemption.
Does not check whether the Department of Health registers your food business instead of the local government (for example businesses on Rottnest Island or in Kings Park, or exporters).
Alfresco dining and signage rules are set by each local government; we show them as things to check.
Does not check development approval for the use of your premises or a fit-out.
Not legal or tax advice. Confirm with the regulator or a qualified professional before you rely on it.

outcomes.title: Register your food business with your local government before you open
outcomes.detail: In WA a food business must not start operating until it is registered with (or has notified) the enforcement agency under the Food Act 2008. For cafes, restaurants, shops, home-based food businesses, manufacturers and food vans that is your local government's environmental health team. Fill in its food business registration form and pay its one-off fee. Food vans register where the van is kept overnight and notify each other local government they trade in.

rules.title: Food safety supervisor
rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified.

outcomes.title: Appoint a certified food safety supervisor and train your food handlers
outcomes.detail: Since 8 December 2023, WA food service, catering and retail businesses that handle unpackaged, potentially hazardous food must meet Food Safety Standard 3.2.2A. You need at least one certified food safety supervisor who is reasonably available, every food handler must be trained, and category one businesses (those that make ready-to-eat food, such as cafes and caterers) must keep records showing key food safety controls for at least 3 months. The supervisor's certificate must be refreshed every 5 years.

rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified.

outcomes.title: You need a WA liquor licence
outcomes.detail: Selling or supplying alcohol in WA needs a licence from Racing, Gaming and Liquor under the Liquor Control Act 1988. Restaurants and small bars apply for a restaurant or small bar licence (A$1,058.50 to apply); taverns and liquor stores cost A$4,129.50 to apply. Every licence then pays an annual fee of A$697.50. One-off events use an occasional licence (from A$62). You also need an approved manager on duty and staff trained in responsible service of alcohol.

rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified.

outcomes.title: Get an alfresco dining (outdoor eating) permit from your local government
outcomes.detail: Putting tables, chairs, A-frame signs or displays on a footpath or other public land in WA needs a permit from your local government under its local laws. Most local governments ask for proof of food business registration, a plan of the area and a public liability certificate (the City of Perth asks for A$20 million cover and charges no fee). Rules, fees and insurance amounts vary by local government. If you serve alcohol in the area, your liquor licence must cover it too.

rules.title: Business signs
rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified.

outcomes.title: Check your local government's rules before you put up signs
outcomes.detail: In WA, signs (advertisements) are controlled by your local government's planning scheme and local planning policies. Many small signs on a shopfront are exempt, but larger, illuminated, pylon or roof signs usually need development approval, and signs on public land need a permit. Check with your local government's planning team before you order signs.

outcomes.title: You must hold workers compensation insurance for your workers
outcomes.detail: Every WA employer must have a workers compensation policy with an approved insurer under the Workers Compensation and Injury Management Act 2023. This includes casual and part-time staff and some contractors, who can count as workers. Get a policy from an approved insurer before your first worker starts. WorkCover WA regulates the scheme and checks that employers are insured.

rules.title: Payroll tax
rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified.

outcomes.title: Check whether you must register for WA payroll tax
outcomes.detail: WA payroll tax applies when your total Australian taxable wages (including those of grouped businesses) are more than A$1 million a year, or A$83,333 in a month. Register with RevenueWA as soon as your wages go over the threshold. The rate is 5.5%, and a diminishing threshold applies to wages between A$1 million and A$7.5 million. With 20 or more staff you are likely to be near or over the threshold.

rule_sets.title: Western Australia: building, painting, plumbing and electrical licences
rule_sets.description: Building contractor and painter registration, home indemnity insurance, plumbing licences and electrical contractor licences for WA trade businesses.
limitations: Built from Building and Energy, Building Services Board and Plumbers Licensing Board pages on wa.gov.au, not from the Building Services (Registration) Act 2011, the Home Building Contracts Act 1991 or the licensing regulations.

Our question about building work uses a A$3,300 line set for Queensland. In WA the building contractor threshold is A$20,000 (A$50,000 for Class 10a buildings such as sheds and carports), so a building job between those amounts is shown as likely, not certain.
Registration only applies in the prescribed area (122 local governments) and where the work needs a building permit; we don't check your location.
Painting is grouped under 'other trade' in our questions, so painter registration is shown as something to check.
Not legal advice. Confirm with Building and Energy (1300 489 099) before you rely on it.

rule_sets.title: Western Australia: tattoo, piercing and beauty businesses
rule_sets.description: Notifying your local government of a skin penetration business and meeting the Health (Skin Penetration Procedures) Regulations 1998 and Code of Practice, from WA Department of Health pages.
limitations: Built from WA Department of Health pages, not from the regulations themselves.
Each local government has its own form, fee and inspection schedule; some also register hairdressing premises under their health local laws.
Lasers (for example for hair or tattoo removal) need a licence under the Radiation Safety Act 1975; we show this as a pointer only.
Cosmetic injectables are regulated as health and medicines matters and are not covered.
Not legal advice. Check with your local government's environmental health team.

outcomes.detail: Tattooing, piercing, scarification, waxing, electrolysis and similar procedures are skin penetration under the Health (Skin Penetration Procedures) Regulations 1998. Before you open, give your local government your trading name, address and the procedures you'll do, with a layout of the premises and fittings. Your premises must meet the Code of Practice for Skin Penetration Procedures, including a hand basin (hands-free in new fit-outs) and separate sinks for hand washing and cleaning equipment. Mobile operators can only work at registered places.

rule_sets.title: Western Australia: licensing and selling imported vehicles
rule_sets.description: Licensing (registering) an imported vehicle with the WA Department of Transport and Major Infrastructure, and the Consumer Protection motor vehicle dealer licence for selling, from WA Government pages.
limitations: Built from Department of Transport and Major Infrastructure and Consumer Protection pages, not from the Road Traffic (Vehicles) Act 2012 or the Motor Vehicle Dealers Act 1973.

Does not cover concessional or club (historic) licensing, or motor vehicle repairer licensing.
Not legal advice. Confirm with the Department of Transport and Major Infrastructure (13 11 56) or Consumer Protection (1300 30 40 54).

rules.title: Licensing the vehicle in WA
rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified.

outcomes.title: Get the vehicle inspected and licensed in WA
outcomes.detail: In WA, registering a vehicle is called licensing it, and you must apply as soon as an imported vehicle arrives. Get a temporary movement permit to drive it to the inspection, pass a roadworthiness inspection (personal effects imports must be inspected by the Department, not an Authorised Inspection Station), then lodge the WA Application to license a vehicle (Form VL17) in person with the Certificate of Inspection, your import approval, ID and proof of purchase. You pay vehicle licence duty on the vehicle's value (2.75% up to A$25,000, rising to 6.5% over A$50,000), the licence fee (A$29.76 per 100 kg for a car, about A$513 a year for a 1,650 kg car) and compulsory motor injury insurance.
